title: Lawsuit filed over death in Regina police scuffle
article: A lawsuit filed Friday on the second anniversary of events that led to a Regina man's death blames a lethal combination of pepper spray and physical restraint by police.

Andrea McLean, the widow of Calvin Roy McLean, is suing the City of Regina and the Regina Police Service. Her 43-year-old husband died on Oct. 9, 2008, hours after going into medical distress during a struggle with police in the 2200 block of Quebec Street near the downtown.
At the time, police said he was conscious immediately after being handcuffed during his late-night arrest on Oct. 8, 2008, but soon suffered a cardiac arrest. He died in hospital the next afternoon.

Because he died while in police custody, McLean's death is to be the subject of a coroner's inquest. On Friday, a Saskatchewan Justice spokesperson said a date for that hearing has still to be set. An inquest will explore the circumstances of the death but not assess blame, and it can make recommendations for preventing such deaths in the future.

While McLean had been pepper sprayed during his arrest, police Chief Troy Hagen told a news conference shortly after the death that, " We can't link necessarily the usage of pepper spray pertaining to this gentleman's current medical condition."

The lawsuit, prepared by lawyer Bob Hrycan, alleges " Mr. McLean died as a direct result of the actions of the defendant in applying an unreasonable and excessive amount of force to him without lawful justification and without reasonable or due care in the circumstances."
A statement of claim is the first step in the civil process and contains allegations not yet proven in court. Statements of defence have yet to be filed.
According to the claim, McLean was distraught over the outcome of a court proceeding in which a family member was a victim of a crime.
Charges had been stayed against one of the two alleged perpetrators.
Police had been in contact with McLean three days before his death because of his distraught state.
"Accordingly when the police arrived ( on Oct. 8), they knew or should have known that Mr. McLean was in a state of agitation and distress and the reasons for such agitation," the claim says.

Police were initially dispatched at around 11: 25 p. m. that night in response to a report of a man armed with an axe. However, the man left and got into a vehicle before police arrived. Police subsequently found the vehicle, but the driver fled on foot. There was a short foot chase, followed by the struggle between police and McLean.

The claim alleges four officers jumped on McLean, restrained him and applied force to his body, including sitting on him. In addition, he was pepper sprayed, " causing him immediate severe distress," the claim says.
The lawsuit alleges that there were no lawful grounds to apply such force and that police didn't take prompt or appropriate steps to obtain medical attention for him.
The suit does not provide a specified amount sought for damages.
